Read relations.py:84-107 (_called_names iterates itertools.pairwise(tokens); requires following.token_type == L_PAREN and token type VAR/IDENTIFIER or token.text.upper() in dialect KEYWORDS). Read sqlglot tokenizer_core.py (installed sqlglot in repo .venv): _scan routes a quote char in self.identifiers (backtick for MySQL, double quote for Postgres) to _scan_identifier (line 1138-1143), which calls _extract_string(identifier_end, escapes) and _add(IDENTIFIER, text) with the unquoted, unescaped text. Unquoted names go through _scan_keywords (826-885): a matched keyword is added as keywords[word] with text=word.upper(), which is in KEYWORDS (so the upper-case-in-keywords branch matches); otherwise _scan_var (1145-1161) adds VAR, or a keyword-mapped type whose upper text is in KEYWORDS; var_single_tokens (e.g. $ for Postgres) keep names like a$b as one VAR. Comments attach to tokens (_scan_comment) and whitespace is skipped, so name /*c*/ ( still yields adjacent token/L_PAREN. Tried the hinted edge (a name in call position tokenizing to a non-VAR/IDENTIFIER type with text outside KEYWORDS): a single-token character cannot start a valid function name, digits start NUMBER (not a valid unquoted routine name); none found. Caveat: read the tokenizer from the repo .venv sqlglot, not the Rust sqlglotrs; the Python core is the specification it mirrors. _called_names collects only from that position.

Traced src/sqllens/safety/relations.py. _called_names (84-107) pairs tokens and collects any VAR/IDENTIFIER/KEYWORD token followed by L_PAREN. sqlglot attaches comments to tokens, so `fn/**/()` still pairs. Backticked or quoted identifiers are IDENTIFIER tokens. Names are returned as written, Python lower() and ASCII-lower. verify_base_tables (122-145) runs the routine check whether or not relations exist, and any non-RlsError failure fails closed. PostgreSQL predicate (236) matches exact or lower(proname), which covers ASCII folding of unquoted names and exact quoted names. Settled so far: the claim holds for ASCII names on PostgreSQL and MySQL. It is unsettled for non-ASCII MySQL names. The query compares LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) with Python-derived strings (245). Python str.lower() and MySQL LOWER() can disagree. For example, 'ΑΣ'.lower() gives final-sigma 'ας', while MySQL would give 'ασ'. Whether the comparison still matches depends on the collation of ROUTINE_NAME and the connection (general_ci may treat the two as equal). I cannot run MySQL here, so I did not run that check. Separately, the MySQL query only matches ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION', so a stored procedure is not matched. A procedure cannot be invoked in a SELECT call position, so the docstring's 'routine' is loose but not clearly wrong. Missing evidence: a live MySQL run of the non-ASCII case-folding comparison.

First half holds: sqlglot parser.py:478 maps "STRPOS" to exp.StrPosition.from_arg_list. Second half is inaccurate. _called_names (relations.py:98-106) collects any token before L_PAREN whose text is in tokenizer KEYWORDS (e.g. IN, DECIMAL), and verify_base_tables (relations.py:124-132) passes them to _refuse_database_routines (relations.py:222-252), which raises RlsError if any non-system pg_proc / information_schema.ROUTINES function shares the name. So a keyword or type name before '(' costs more than a catalog match: if the database defines a routine named e.g. decimal, any statement using DECIMAL( is refused. The docstring's 'only cost a catalog match' omits this possible refusal (fail-closed, rare, but the stated cost is wrong).

relations.py:91-92 docstring says PostgreSQL 'folds only ASCII in unquoted names'. PostgreSQL's downcase_identifier (scansup.c) also lower-cases high-bit bytes via tolower() when the database encoding is single-byte (e.g. LATIN1: unquoted Äfn folds to äfn). So the absolute statement is wrong for single-byte server encodings. Code at 104-106 returns as-written, str.lower() and ASCII-lower spellings, and the predicate at 236 also matches lower(proname), so the guard likely still covers such cases in practice, but the docstring rationale is inaccurate (true only for multibyte encodings such as UTF-8). Comment-only defect.

sql_runner.py:61-65,140-142,169 imports and connects with psycopg2 and passes that conn to verify_base_tables(conn, sql, dialect='postgres'). relations.py:127 uses a default connection.cursor(); relations.py:232-239 executes with (names, names), where names is a non-empty list[str] (guarded at relations.py:125,131). psycopg2 adapts a Python list of str to ARRAY['a','b'], so `proname::text = ANY(%s)` and `lower(proname::text) = ANY(%s)` compare text against a text array. Each %s gets its own copy of the list, so using it twice is fine. This is documented psycopg2 behaviour (lists adapt to ARRAY; `= ANY(%s)` is the recommended idiom).

relations.py:240-252: the mysql branch runs SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.ROUTINES WHERE ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION' AND LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (...) LIMIT 1, and raises RlsError iff cursor.fetchone() is not None; no row means no raise (call allowed). Names come from _called_names (lines 85-107), which yields as-written, lower and ASCII-lower forms. Visibility: ROUTINES lists only routines the user defined or has EXECUTE-level privilege on. Calling a stored function needs EXECUTE (or being the definer). So any function the SQL Lens user can invoke is listed and refused, and an unlisted routine cannot be executed, so allowing it on a missing row is safe. Hostile input considered: a function the user can call yet is unlisted. I found none, since the privilege that permits the call also governs listing. I read this from MySQL documentation knowledge, not by running MySQL.

relations.py:165-189 runs EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM pg_catalog.pg_inherits i WHERE i.inhrelid = c.oid) per relation and raises TypeError for a non-bool flag. PostgreSQL's pg_inherits stores one row per direct child->parent link (inhrelid = child oid, inhparent = parent oid), for both inheritance and declarative partitioning, including sub-partitions. A grandchild has its own row naming itself as inhrelid, so EXISTS is true at any depth. The cursor is a plain connection.cursor() (relations.py:127), not a dict cursor, so row[3] is a tuple element. psycopg2's default boolean typecaster returns Python bool. The positional row[3] access is valid, and the bool-or-TypeError guard fails closed. Both dependencies hold. This rests on PostgreSQL and psycopg2 documented behavior, not on a run against a live database.

PostgreSQL records every inheritance/partition link as a pg_inherits row (inhrelid=child, inhparent=direct parent), so a grandchild (e.g. a leaf under a sub-partition) has its own row with its direct parent, just like a direct child; this holds for relkind r, p and f (foreign-table partitions) children. src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:167 queries EXISTS on pg_inherits i WHERE i.inhrelid = c.oid, which relies on this (one row per child at any depth), and :177 applies it for kinds r/p (_BASE_TABLE_KINDS line 50); other kinds fall to the base-table refusal at :216, which does not contradict the comment. The test (tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:515-516) models orders_2024 and orders_2024_q1 both with is_child True. Absolute-claim trace: sub-partition 'p' child and 'f' partition both have inhrelid rows; views/matviews cannot be inheritance children, so the comment's scope is accurate.

criteria.json is a list of {criterion,text} objects and carries criterion 2, so it counts. Read src/sqllens/safety/relations.py and safety/__init__.py at head. Execution path: RlsGuardRunner.run_sql (__init__.py:162-200) rewrites via apply_rls, then if rules exist passes options require_base_tables=True (line 197) regardless of database.read_only, and calls the inner runner with the REWRITTEN sql (line 199). The pg/mysql runners call verify_base_tables(conn, args.sql, dialect=...) when require_base_tables (postgres/sql_runner.py:168-169, mysql/sql_runner.py:137-138), before executing. So the names checked are those of the post-rewrite SQL. _called_names (relations.py:84-107) tokenizes with the dialect tokenizer and collects any token followed by L_PAREN that is VAR, IDENTIFIER (quoted) or an upper-case member of tokenizer KEYWORDS; it does not rely on typed function nodes, so strpos-style renamed built-ins and keyword names like replace are covered. Schema-qualified calls work since the token before ( is the bare name. Select list, FROM, joins, filters, aggregates, window functions all yield tokens identically. Names emitted as text, lower(), and ASCII-lower. verify_base_tables (122-134): early return only when there are no relations AND no called names, so relation-free statements still reach the lookup. _refuse_database_routines (222-252): PostgreSQL queries pg_proc joined to pg_namespace excluding pg_catalog and information_schema, matching proname or lower(proname) against names, no schema or signature restriction (extension routines are pg_proc entries in non-system schemas); MySQL queries information_schema.ROUTINES with ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION' and LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN names. Any row raises RlsError. Name-only matching across schemas/signatures confirmed. Trace of absolute-style input: quoted mixed-case routine "MyFn" called as MYFN( -> names include 'myfn'; lower(proname)='myfn' matches; refused. Schema-qualified s.f( and f ( with comments/whitespace tokenise the same.
Split conditions: (a) `dialect in ('postgres','mysql')` false (sqlite) -> outside the trigger (criterion limited to PostgreSQL or MySQL; sibling criterion 7 says SQLite runs no routine lookup). (b) `not relations and not called` early return -> outside the trigger: it fires only when no token is in call position, so no call exists to refuse. (c) token filter skipping tokens not followed by L_PAREN, or not VAR/IDENTIFIER/keyword, or empty text -> outside the trigger: such tokens are not call-syntax names. (d) except Exception fallback in verify_base_tables (137-145) -> fault alternative (lookup/parse error) that fails closed with RlsError; criterion 6 names it. (e) cursor.fetchone() None -> no matching routine, so no refusal, correct per the criterion. Non-ASCII case-folding differences cannot make an unquoted/quoted PG call resolve to a differently-cased routine, so no gap found. MySQL visibility is limited to what information_schema.ROUTINES lists, which is exactly the claim's wording.

docs/external/row-level-security.md:164 contains the quoted text. PostgreSQL docs (xfunc-sql, 'SQL Functions on Composite Types') say a function taking a composite/table row type can be called as attribute notation `table.function` (e.g. `SELECT o.order_total FROM orders o` resolves to order_total(o)) when no column of that name exists. PostgreSQL's GRANT/default privileges docs say EXECUTE on functions is granted to PUBLIC by default, so revoking it from PUBLIC is the right instruction. Both are from my knowledge of the PostgreSQL docs; I did not fetch them in this run. The claim is an authored doc statement, and it is accurate.
